claims.text: A two-step heat treatment consisting of high-temperature homogenization followed by low-temperature aging can control phase evolution in Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni HEAs.
The two-step treatment induces controlled precipitation of coherent ordered phases such as B2.
The as-cast or rapidly quenched alloy is predominantly disordered FCC or a mixed disordered structure with minimal precipitates.
Homogenization at about 1200 degrees Celsius for several hours dissolves microsegregation and produces chemical uniformity.
Aging Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys at temperatures in the 600-750 degrees Celsius range for about 20 hours followed by rapid quenching is a viable thermal-processing step.
The thermal treatment should be conducted under inert gas or vacuum to prevent oxidation.
A treatment of 1200 degrees Celsius for 5 hours followed by 650 degrees Celsius for 20 hours is an appropriate example schedule.
The structural mediator is a population of coherent ordered precipitates, such as B2, within a disordered matrix.
High-temperature treatment erases chemical inhomogeneity in the alloy.
Low-temperature aging drives an ordering transformation.
Aging transforms part of the matrix into fine, coherent ordered precipitates.
The coherent precipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
Precipitation strengthening increases strength while retaining sufficient ductility.
The treated alloy develops a dual-phase microstructure comprising a continuous disordered matrix and finely dispersed coherent ordered precipitates.
The treatment increases yield strength and hardness while preserving balanced ductility relative to the as-cast alloy.
The baseline as-cast or rapidly quenched alloy is chemically homogeneous, largely disordered, and has little to no tailored precipitation.
The beneficial effect is likely limited to compositions near equiatomic ratios.
Mechanical behavior and phase evolution are sensitive to aging temperature.
Improper aging temperature or time may cause over-aging or formation of coarse or brittle phases.
Precipitate volume fraction, coherence, and mechanical-property changes depend on processing parameters and require experimental optimization.

contradictions.description: The initial state and baseline are described as chemically homogeneous, while the proposed homogenization step is said to be necessary to eliminate microsegregation and chemical inhomogeneity.
